When many developers start developing a mobile app, they decide to use a language that only works on one of the two operating systems. These languages have different syntax and grammar, but they run faster and can look like other apps on the device.

Other developers use a third programming language, to develop apps for both platforms. However, these languages generally don't run as fast and apps made with them don't look like they belong on the device. Sometimes, these apps don't even work on both devices as promised.

For this reason, if a developer doesn't have a lot of time or money they may opt to make the app natively for one platform. Then once they have more money, make it for a second platform.
As a dev currently working on a Voat app (android only), this sums up the point beautifully.

I'm a novice at programming but I'll try to do my best to explain.

Programming is fairly consistent across languages, but the structure is different. Sure all the if/thens are gonna be the same, and you can just copy+paste textures and assets, but the structure of the code is completely different. While it does the same thing, changing between two languages requires that you change the way that your app works internally.

Say you have a pizza store and you want to open another one in a different location. What will be the same is the content (which represents the assets and graphics and such). In both locations, the same types of pizza, wings, and soft drinks will be sold. What's different is the structure. Since it's the same store, it'll be the same type of thing up front: you'll go up to the counter and order your food. But maybe you enter from the left instead of the right, or something small. The big difference will be internally -- say the kitchen is shaped differently, so the cooks take a different route from the fridge to the prep table to the oven to the counter. While the end result looks the same to you, the internals are built differently so it must be handled in a different way. That's why the apps are different. Sure there's all the same stuff on the inside, but it's arranged differently so you have to work differently in order to accommodate the way that it's internally arranged.

I hope this helps. Anybody that knows what they're talking about feel free to correct me if I'm wrong.

Well, Billy. You know how you like Pokemon? Well, if you wanted to make your own Squirtle to bring to show-and-tell, you could do it by building it out of Lego, or you could use your clay. Both would be a Squirtle, but you would make them out of different things.

If you want to make programs for the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store, you have to use different computer languages. Making apps for these stores are kind of like making a Squirtle for show-and-tell. If you're making it for Google, you have to use Java, which is kind of like using clay. If you're making it for Apple, you have to use Objective-C, which is kind of like using Lego. You're making the same thing, but it's different. You have to plan how you're going to build differently depending on what you're building with. You can't just turn Lego into Clay. You can make a copy that looks similar, but it will be build differently.

Hello everyone,

I just saw this sub pop up and I was wondering if anyone had any advice for a recently graduated student. I'm sure others have or are going to feel this at some point and I was hoping you could help me and maybe provide some help to the next person who feels this way after graduation.

All through our courses at university we have a set list of what we have to do next. Each week is planned out. Even when we are working on our own we have a set idea of how things need to go and when they are due by. However now that I am done with school and received my degree I feel, well for a lack of better term, listless. I wake up and go about my routine. I go to my internship and work, I come home and rest and play videogames. But I can't shake this feeling of emptiness and no clue of what I should be doing. Like a goal was achieved and instead of feeling happy about it I feel this overpowering sadness and drifting. I know everyone says that this is the time we are too look for jobs, plan our lives, and get everything done. But I can't even seem to get the energy and feeling to even start. For the first time in my life the next step isn't clear, and instead of things not being planned feeling liberating, it is almost crippling.

So for those who have graduated, and those who will be graduating, how do you fend off the post-graduation blues and figure out the next step? Is this normal, or is it a fluke and just me? What is some advice you would give me and people who are feeling like me about what to do now that the "party is over".
How To Deal With The Post-Graduation Blues

Get out of your comfort zone. If there's anything you've wanted to pursue but didn't have the time to before or just haven't done it, start now. Meet people, learn new crafts and skills, etc, just never stop learning. Education certainly does not end when you're done with school. Also, you're (probably) still very young, and don't forget that. You'll still make mistakes and fuck shit up, but be smart about how you handle it afterwards.

Don't get "old" in the brain. Believe me, the party is FAR from over.
